description: LLMs, AI-assisted coding, ML basics for devs

screens.body:
AI is the biggest shift in how software gets built since the internet. But here's the calm truth: AI doesn't replace developers — it changes what developers spend time on. You stop typing boilerplate and spend more time deciding what to build and checking that it's right.

Think of it like a power tool. A power drill doesn't replace the carpenter — it just means she spends her skill on design and precision instead of turning screws by hand.

options: A power tool that changes where you spend your skill
A replacement for developers
Just a trend you can ignore
check.question: AI in software is best thought of as…

screens.heading: AI is a power tool, not a replacement
screens.keyPoint: AI changes where your skill goes, not whether you're needed.

screens.body:
LLM stands for Large Language Model. It's software trained on enormous amounts of text — books, code, websites — until it learns the patterns of how language (and code) fits together.

When you prompt one, it doesn't 'know' the answer. It predicts the most likely next piece of text, one token at a time. That's why it can write shockingly good code and also confidently invent a library that doesn't exist.

options: Looking up answers in a database
Predicting the most likely next piece of text
Running your code to see what happens
check.question: An LLM generates text by…

screens.heading: What an LLM actually is
screens.keyPoint: Prediction, not knowledge — impressive and fallible.

screens.body:
AI-assisted coding tools — Copilot, Cursor, Claude — sit inside your editor and help you write code. They autocomplete lines, explain confusing code, and can even scaffold whole features from a prompt.

You already use this: Cursor helped build Learn SD. The trick is staying the driver. You describe the goal, it drafts, and you review every line like a senior dev reviewing a junior's pull request.

options: You describe the goal, it drafts, you review everything
It writes the app and you ship it unreviewed
It replaces your IDE
check.question: The healthy way to use AI coding tools:

screens.heading: AI-assisted coding
screens.keyPoint: You drive. AI drafts. You review.

screens.body:
Good prompts have three ingredients: context (what the code does, the stack, the constraints), a specific task (one thing, not five), and the format you want back (a function, an explanation, a diff).

Bad: 'fix my code.' Good: 'This Express route should return 404 when the user isn't found, but it crashes instead. Here's the route and the error…' Specificity is the whole game.

options: Keep it vague so it can be creative
Type in all caps
Give context, one specific task, and the format you want
check.question: What makes a prompt effective?

screens.heading: Prompting: the new literacy
screens.keyPoint: Context + one specific task + desired format.

screens.body:
Because models predict patterns, they hallucinate: plausible-sounding code that uses fake functions, outdated APIs, or subtle logic bugs. This isn't rare — it's the default failure mode.

So the rule is simple: never ship AI-written code you couldn't explain yourself. Run it, test it, read it. The model is a fast intern, not an authority.

options: It's always correct
It can hallucinate — plausible but wrong code
It only works for Python
check.question: The default failure mode of AI-generated code:

screens.heading: Hallucinations: trust, then verify
screens.keyPoint: Fast intern, not authority. Run it, read it, test it.

screens.body:
Machine learning is the broader field behind all this. The core loop is simple: feed a model lots of examples (training), then ask it to predict on new inputs (inference). Spam filters, recommendations, image search — all the same loop.

As a dev, you rarely train models from scratch. You use trained ones through APIs — like Byte in Learn SD calling Gemini. Knowing the loop helps you understand costs, latency, and why outputs vary.

options: Training on examples, then predicting on new inputs
Memorizing a textbook
Only used by researchers
check.question: The ML loop is…

screens.heading: ML basics for developers
screens.keyPoint: Train on examples, predict on new ones — usually via API.

screens.body:
Where does AI fit in YOUR work? Three places: in your editor (Cursor/Copilot while you build), in your products (Byte the tutor calls the Gemini API), and in your process (drafting docs, summarizing, debugging help).

You don't need a PhD. You need API literacy: how to call a model, how to keep keys secret, how to handle wrong answers gracefully in your UI — like Byte's fallback when no key is set.

options: Training your own models from scratch
Getting a PhD first
Calling AI APIs well and handling imperfect answers

screens.keyPoint: API literacy beats model-building for app devs.
